rv.q: This karaoke comedy about warped-vinyl dreams is about as guilty as pleasures get.
The show is a cheerfully shameless pastiche of '80s arena rock that manages to be both knowing and innocent at the same time.

All of which makes "Rock of Ages" a somewhat glib trip against the colorful, chaotic nostalgia of Broadway's genuine homage to '80s metal - but it's breezy, silly fun, and a hair-metal musical has yet to be written.
This cheesy exercise in rock nostalgia has already been a hit in Los Angeles and Off-Broadway, and this transfer to the Rialto should prove an equally critic-proof success.

This jukebox musical featuring vintage rock tunes from the likes of Twisted Sister and Bon Jovi is sure to turn off some theater purists. But it's so cleverly staged and impressively performed that it's an irresistible, offbeat trip of a show that hits all the right notes.
But it's frequently more fun than it has any right to be.
But the humor level is so low and the characters so broad that interest in the story is lost after the first 20 minutes.
Now on the Great White Way the show is all amped up volume with postured manic cliches that feels stuck in a rut.
But the guilty pleasures offered by the music are diminished by the irritatingly self-conscious, irony-drenched presentation.
For the first time, we are asked to review Noise.
It's a huge break from last week's 'Prometheus' -all you have to do is sit back and surrender to the almighty cheese.
When was the last time you were encouraged to drink beer during a Broadway show? Or, for that matter, wave (fake) lighters during power ballads and occasionally sing along?

cn.t: Critics are divided on this '80s hair-metal jukebox musical, with some finding it absurdly enjoyable and cleverly staged, while others dismiss it as campy noise with a paper-thin plot that substitutes winking self-awareness for genuine charm.
